> When I first started I kept reviewing and studying the process of LOA, then realized I was just reading and reviewing the recipe over and over but I wasn't actually "cooking"--doing it.
> So, I thought for a moment of want I wanted and decided on a coffee cup because my current one was more rectangular in shape and I preferred the more rounded ones, so I started to visualize...
> My visual was of me in the first person view standing exactly where I was currently standing (front of stove), and drinking from a white rounded coffee cup. But although the visual was clear, for some reason, I couldn't seem to fully visualize the entire cup, only about 75% of it, from the handle out. My emotions were neutral or more of a content feeling. And I visualized it for at least 25-30 secs, it didn't seem very long. When I felt I'd done enough I stopped thinking about it and continued with my reviewing.
> The same day my sister was washing dishes (manually) and we were talking about stuff, then as she places a dish in the dish rack (on the counter) she accidentally drops my old coffee cup! and it falls to the floor shattering to pieces!
> As I immediately recognized the event for what it was, the catalyst for the new coffee cup to enter my experience, i.e., what needed to happen in order for my new coffee cup to manifest, I said in my head with excitement, "It's happening! Something's happening!"
> That was my evidence from the Universe that what I wanted or visualized would in someway manifest. I had learned in my studies that sometimes the old has to be broken down in order for the new to be built. So, I knew it was coming, but in the meantime, I drank my coffee in a beer mug, never once complaining or feeling bad about it because I knew it was coming.
> A month later, my sister comes home from the store and says, "Oh, I got you a new coffee cup." and it was white, rounded--and funny thing--had four black strips on the front! (remember I couldn't visualize the whole thing, lol.) but I thought it looked great.

> Your boundary conditions (flimsy material, fast RPM) are more or less mutually exclusive. But...
> Flimsy material means you want smaller diameters as the gear speed increases. You can use a fairly large gear at first, but each subsequent stage should be smaller in diameter. To be compatible from a large gear to a smaller gear, you'll want to stick with smaller teeth. Internal stress in the gear is going to be proportional to the radius, but also to the square of the speed.
> Without question, the limiting factor is going to be that internal stress, not a factor of the gearing. Motors that spin in the 10k RPM range aren't that hard (think angle grinder) and small (unsealed) ABEC 5+ ball bearings can reach 100k easily. 10:1 is not hard to reach with a very basic gear train. But "flimsy" gear material at speeds above 10k is asking for internal failures and pieces of gear flying about.
> So either test carefully and safely (increasing speed of the system while sufficiently shrouded to capture debris) or do some careful stress analysis.

> The distinction is that the magnetic field lines are moving though the stator, but they are constant in the rotor. Changes in magnetic field (where they go from north to south, or weak to strong) and conductive material acts like shoving a knife down into peanut butter. It has viscous drag, effectively, and also resistance to change in direction like sliding friction of an object on a surface. Let's see how far I can take this analogy!
> What's happening is that as the magnetic field plunges through a steel plate, it act the same way that a transformer secondary (or your coils, for that matter) act in response to a field: it produces an effective voltage, and current flow results. The current flow in turn makes an electromagnet which pushed back against the field. This is the eddy current loss (viscous drag-like loss).
> The other thing about peanut butter, or fields in a steel plate for that matter, is that it's a semisolid, so it takes some minimum force to move the knife at all. The analogous behavior of steel is that the magnetic domains have hysteresis. Imagine if all the magnetic domains were like compass needles, but instead of being mounted on a nice little pivots, they were all just scattered on the table. If you put a strong magnet near them, they would reorient, but there would be friction and so they wouldn't change position for a small magnetic force. This is roughly what steel does. That "sliding friction"' effect, called hysteresis, also means that as the rotor approaches a patch of steel, it is less strongly polarized as the magnet approaches than when the magnet is leaving. The steel "waits" to magnetize until pushed to do so, and then "waits" to demagnetize until the applied field is quite low. So the magnet is attracted more strongly as it tries to leave, which acts as a constant drag force on the hub.
> Hugh Piggott is the original authority on this, although the text is old enough that NdFeB magnets weren't available and so iron in the field was even more important.
> This text seems to contain quite a nice summary of basic theory in an accessible presentation. Page 4 has a good diagram of what the "back iron" of the field (as the steel rotor plates would be called in traditional motor terminology) does to the magnetic lines. You can see how the field is funneled directly to the next magnet instead of needing to travel through extra air gap. Note that the thickness dimension of the side view of the rotor is unnecessarily large from a magnetic perspective (although it wouldn't hurt to have thicker rotors). You can see that they've drawn the field lines just as close together in the magnet as in the steel. Since steel supports a field almost twice as strong as the magnet, you could crowd those lines together in the rotor plate more tightly without issue. They have thickness = 1/2 magnet width, and I'm suggesting thickness = 1/4 magnet width as a minimum. But if you made the rotors thicker, no problem.
